Understand the risk calculator

A worked example shows why the loss budget comes before leverage and position size.

Contract Compass guide · Updated November 6, 2026

The calculator works backward from a loss budget. It estimates a quantity whose loss at the scenario’s stop, plus assumed entry and exit costs, stays within that budget after rounding down to the contract’s lot step. It does not recommend how much money you should risk.

Start with a hypothetical loss budget

Suppose a fictional account has 1,000 USDT, and you enter 0.5% as the risk per trade. The calculator’s budget is 5 USDT. This is a numerical example, not advice to use that percentage or to open a trade.

Now suppose the example entry is 100 USDT and the stop reference is 99 USDT. The price distance is 1 USDT per unit. Dividing 5 by 1 would give five units if trading were free. The app also includes estimated fees and slippage, so the actual quantity is smaller.

Costs change the quantity

With a fee assumption of 0.05% per side and slippage of 0.02% per side, estimated cost per unit is (100 + 99) × 0.07%, or 0.1393 USDT. Total modeled risk per unit is 1.1393 USDT.

For an illustrative lot step of 0.01, 5 ÷ 1.1393 rounded down to that step is 4.38 units. Modeled loss at the stop is about 4.99 USDT, position value is 438 USDT, and approximate initial margin at 2× leverage is 219 USDT. Real contracts can have different steps and minimums.

Leverage does not improve the setup

Changing leverage changes the estimated money set aside as margin. It does not improve the breakout, move the stop, increase the loss budget, or make the scenario’s reward/risk ratio better. A larger leverage setting can leave less room before liquidation.

The initial-margin output is approximate. The app does not calculate exchange maintenance-margin tiers or liquidation price. A stop reference does not guarantee an exit before liquidation.

Why a calculator result is not a live signal

You can inspect a quantity for either scenario even when the primary decision says Watch or Wait. The calculator labels these cases as illustrations. A valid arithmetic result does not supply missing technical confirmation.

Read affordability and minimum-size warnings. The estimated margin plus opening costs may exceed the entered balance, or the rounded quantity may fail an exchange minimum. Avoid increasing risk simply to clear a minimum.

What the estimate leaves out

Funding, price gaps, delayed execution, changing liquidity, and liquidation can make realized losses greater than the displayed estimate. Fee defaults are assumptions, not a statement of your account tier. Entering optimistic costs does not remove those costs from a real trade.

The balance and calculator inputs stay in page memory and are not sent to Binance, analytics, or advertising. The calculator does not place orders or save a trading account. CFTC: risks of virtual-currency trading. For the live-data checks behind a scenario, read Data freshness and limitations.
